author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Guest Who Stayed
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
Greg arrived at Tideglass Cove with two broken folding chairs and an unfinished song.

I knew the song was unfinished because he'd hummed the same four notes through the Starwake Door, across the square, and down the steps to the beach without finding a fifth.

Maui heard him before I did.

"Is that music," he asked, "or is someone being chased by a very polite goat?"

Greg looked offended for a second.

Then he laughed.

"Little of both."

He set the chairs beside the workshop. One had a bent hinge. The other wobbled because a screw had stripped the wood beneath its bracket.

"These are for the rest bench by the sea-glass orchard," he explained. "Pip said the older ones weren't comfortable for people waiting for the ferry."

Maui lifted the wobbly chair.

"I can fix that."

Greg reached for the other.

"Hey, I've got tools."

Maui flexed his shoulders.

"I can carry both."

"Great, but can you fix both?"

"I can do anything."

I closed my eyes.

Here we went.

They were both trying to be kind. That was the problem. Maui wanted to be the helpful hero; Greg wanted to be the man who showed up when a job needed doing. Neither had asked the person who'd requested the chairs what the job actually involved.

Pip arrived carrying a folded sketch.

"Good, you're here," they said.

"We've got it," Maui announced.

"Do you?" Pip asked.

Greg held up a screwdriver.

"Mostly."

Pip unfolded the sketch.

The bench needed two chairs with stable seats and backs at slightly different heights. One person using the sheltered garden found it difficult to stand from the low seat. Another wanted armrests they could grip. The chairs also had to fit on the path without blocking anyone using wheels or a handcart.

Neither broken chair was the right size.

Maui looked at the drawing.

Greg looked at the chairs.

I bit the inside of my cheek to stop smiling.

"Maybe we should ask the person who needs them," I said.

Pip nodded.

"That was my next sentence."

We found Ilya, the garden steward's assistant, checking the first sea-kale bed. They had been the one to request seating because they spent long stretches weeding and sometimes needed to rest before walking back uphill.

"These are too low," Ilya said when we showed the chairs.

Greg examined the legs.

"I could add blocks."

"That might make them unstable," Ilya said. "And the path is narrow here."

Maui put the chairs down.

"What would help?"

Ilya looked surprised.

"A bench with a firm seat and two armrests. Nothing fancy. I want to sit without sinking into it, and I want to be able to stand without somebody having to pull me up."

Maui nodded.

"Then let's build that."

Pip smiled.

"Now we're talking."

The afternoon became a lesson in designing for the person who would use the thing, rather than the person who wanted the satisfaction of finishing it.

Tamsin provided measurements. Edda checked the turning space. Ilya tested a temporary model made from a crate and two spare boards. Greg sanded the edges. Maui held the supports while the screws went in.

I watched them work, amused by how quickly the competition dissolved once there was an actual specification.

Then Greg started humming again.

Four notes. A pause. Four notes.

Maui looked at him.

"What's that song about?"

Greg shrugged.

"Coming back to a place that's changed."

"Sounds sad."

"Some of it is."

"Make it heroic."

Greg laughed.

"That's one option."

Maui began proposing lyrics involving storms, monsters, and the triumph of returning across a thousand seas. Greg tried the rhythm out of politeness. It was terrible.

I told them so.

"Both of you are making the song about the loudest person in the room," I said.

Greg looked at me.

"Who should it be about?"

"I don't know. It's your song."

Maui folded his arms.

"You said it was terrible."

"It was. I didn't say you have to let me write it."

Greg smiled.

"Fair."

They sat beside the unfinished bench while Ilya tested the armrest. For a few minutes nobody spoke.

Then Greg played the four notes again, softer.

Ilya paused.

"That sounds like the ferry bell," they said.

Greg looked up.

"The what?"

"The little bell Fen rings when the tide turns and the upper path is open. It's not exciting. It just tells people when to come back."

Greg stared at the water.

Then he played a fifth note.

It fit.

Maui looked at Ilya.

"That's what the song needed?"

"Maybe."

Greg smiled.

"Maybe."

We finished the bench before sunset. Ilya sat on it, stood without help, and sat again. Edda checked the path clearance and approved the location. The old chairs went back to Starwake for salvageable parts instead of being placed where they would be inconvenient.

Pip wrote a maintenance note for the next month's inspection.

Maui looked at the finished bench.

"No plaque?"

"No plaque," I said.

"Not even a small one?"

Pip handed him a pencil.

"You may write the inspection date underneath."

He did.

Greg stood beside the bench with his guitar.

"Can I play the song here when it's done?"

Ilya considered the question.

"As long as you ask before you turn the orchard into a concert."

"Deal."

The evening air was cool. The tide had come in enough to cover the old stones where the second bell had sounded. The temporary closure sign remained in place. Someone had drawn a tiny crab in the corner.

Maui slipped an arm around my shoulders.

"Greg's not bad," he said.

"He's not."

"Bit slow with the monsters."

"Not every song needs one."

Maui grinned.

"Are you sure?"

Greg joined us on the path and looked between us.

"You two have any plans for dinner?"

"I was going to ask Jasper if they'd like to come home," Maui said.

Greg looked at me rather than assuming an answer.

"I was going to ask if you'd be free tomorrow to hear the new chorus. No pressure."

I appreciated the difference. The relationships in my life did not have to turn every shared evening into a contest or a secret. Maui knew Greg and I cared about each other. Greg knew Maui mattered to me. Neither of them had to become anything more to the other for that to be true.

"Tomorrow afternoon works," I said. "Tonight I'm going home with Maui."

Greg smiled.

"Great. I'll bring the fifth note."

Maui looked at him.

"Make it a heroic one."

"Maybe a modestly heroic one."

They laughed.

On the way home, Maui was quiet for a while.

"Did I make that awkward?" he asked.

"A little."

He winced.

"You were trying to help. So was Greg. Ilya needed both of you to listen first."

Maui thought about the bench.

"I think I'm getting better."

"You are."

He squeezed my hand.

"Does that make me less impressive?"

I stopped, turned toward him, and kissed his cheek.

"No. It makes you easier to love."

He blushed.

The great Maui, who had bragged about lassoing the sun, blushed beside a public bench.

I decided not to mention it.

At home, he carved a second tiny fish into the broom handle. This one looked suspiciously like Greg's hair.

I made him promise not to give it to Greg without asking.

He promised.

Mostly.
